title: Listening to the Experts Doesn't Mean Giving Them the Last Word
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos explores how teachers should relate to expert research, arguing that teachers keep the last word in the classroom but only if they have been trained to evaluate evidence. Drawing on Carnine, Dykstra, Hendrick and Hewitt and Sachdeva, she contends that education behaves like a belief-based profession and that translating research from lab to lesson is hard but necessary. Her own journey with orthographic mapping, through Dehaene, Ehri, Seidenberg and Gentry and Ouellette, illustrates how expertise informs rather than constrains professional judgment. She responds to a whole-language commenter who treats teacher autonomy as untouchable and contrasts science-based and sentiment-based language about teacher education. She concludes that autonomy without knowledge is a pernicious ploy and that teacher training should equip teachers to separate snake oil from well-supported argument. The piece is mostly assembled from long quotations, but the framing argument is her own.
points: Teachers cannot act on what they do not know exists, so training and PD must supply research knowledge that classroom experience alone will not.
Evidence-informed guidance informs rather than constrains professional judgment, and teachers should be taught to evaluate research claims themselves.
Autonomy without knowledge is a pernicious ploy, yet blind deference to experts is also unwise, since experts can be wrong.
Objective, evidence-based language about teacher training differs sharply from sentiment-driven language that can deny students systematic instruction.
quotes: Children are not born with an innate ability to read, and teachers are not born with an innate ability to teach. We have to know our subject-matter and learn how best to teach it, which is why one college professor opined that kindergarten teachers should be the highest paid instructors, K-College.

The problem with this stance is that a teacher, like all other mere mortals, doesn’t know what they don’t know. I couldn’t have restructured my lessons to promote orthographic mapping until I learned of its existence as well as its importance—and how it is supported by research in neuroscience, educational psychology, and cognitive psychology.

This is a stark illustration of how we practitioners are not just pulling lessons out of a hat or thin air. For better or worse, we are dependent upon outside training to complement inside experience. However, too often, we are insufficiently trained and negatively influenced by ‘experts’ espousing unsubstantiated theories that might make us feel a certain way about our subject and our students—the sentiment—but at the expense of misrepresenting the reality of robust research—the science—that should guide our decision-making.

Authority comes from learning our trade and the tricks of that trade—informed by research but reshaped by classroom experience. Granting autonomy devoid of professional responsibility is a pernicious ploy because we don’t just gain knowledge from experience—we gain it from learning something new.

I am not an outlier: any expertise that I have, like all expertise, has come from continuous training in concepts related to teaching and learning. However, the fact that I have independently pursued this training is an accident of temperament and not an example of a desired protocol for best practices in professional development. We abandon our responsibility to our teachers when we turn our back on training them to train themselves: imparting knowledge but also instilling in them the ability to separate the snake oil from the logic of a well-oiled argument that is supported by research.

Balance also matters, balancing expertise with experience: a reliance on rigor from teacher education programs and professional development, but a recognition that application to the classroom is always contextualized by the students we have in front of us.
